topic.subject: general
topic.title: Junk food and sugar
topic.scope: hidden sugar in drinks, salt and fried snacks, energy drinks, diabetes risk, myths that fruit juice equals fruit

nodes.name: Sugar hides in sauces and 'healthy' foods
Sugar has other names on labels
Free sugar should be under about 10% of energy
One can of cola holds many teaspoons of sugar
Salt is in processed food, not only added at table
Trans and saturated fats raise heart risk
Juice has less fibre than the fruit
Packaged juice often has added sugar

Energy drinks do not replace food or water
Type 2 diabetes links to diet and weight

Thin people can also have unhealthy diets
Too much salt raises blood pressure

misconceptions.statement: Cold drinks are mostly flavoured water, so they have very little sugar.
misconceptions.why: Drinks look like clear liquid and do not feel like solid sweets.
misconceptions.fix: A typical 300 ml cold drink has about 30 g sugar, roughly 7 to 8 teaspoons.

probe.question: A 300 ml cold drink bottle has about how much sugar?
probe.wrong_answer: Hardly any, 1 or 2 grams, since it is mostly water.

misconceptions.root_belief: what is liquid or invisible has little content

misconceptions.why: Students link sugar with taste alone.
misconceptions.fix: Tomato ketchup, sauces, flavoured yoghurt and biscuits have added sugar even if not very sweet.

probe.question: Does tomato ketchup contain added sugar?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it tastes sour and spicy, so no sugar.

misconceptions.statement: Fruit juice is just as healthy as eating the whole fruit.
misconceptions.why: Students see juice as 'made from fruit' and assume the nutrition is identical, ignoring what is lost when fruit is squeezed.
misconceptions.fix: Juice has most of the fibre removed and its sugar becomes 'free sugar' that is absorbed quickly. Whole fruit is more filling and healthier; WHO advises limiting juice.

probe.question: Is a glass of orange juice as healthy as eating an orange?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both are the same because juice is made from the orange.

misconceptions.root_belief: Processing a natural food does not change its nutrition
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO sugar guideline; ICMR-NIN dietary guidelines

misconceptions.statement: Energy drinks give real energy and can replace food or water after sports.
misconceptions.why: The name 'energy drink' and sports advertising suggest it fuels the body better than meals or water.
misconceptions.fix: Energy drinks mostly contain sugar and caffeine. They give a short boost, do not replace meals or water, and are not recommended for children.

probe.question: After a football match, what is best to drink to refill your body?
probe.wrong_answer: An energy drink, because it gives more energy than water.

misconceptions.root_belief: Product names and advertisements describe true benefits

misconceptions.statement: Energy drinks are safe for children because they are sold in shops like other drinks.
misconceptions.why: Students assume anything freely sold is safe for all ages.
misconceptions.fix: Energy drinks contain high caffeine and sugar, which can cause sleeplessness, fast heartbeat and anxiety in children. FSSAI requires warning labels and advises against use by children.

probe.question: Can a 12-year-old safely drink an energy drink every day?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is sold openly so it is safe for everyone.

misconceptions.root_belief: If a product is sold freely, it is safe

misconceptions.statement: Salt only affects people who are old.
misconceptions.why: Students link blood pressure problems with old age and think children need not worry about salt.
misconceptions.fix: Eating too much salt raises blood pressure at any age, and food habits formed in childhood continue later. WHO advises less than 5 g of salt a day for adults, and less for children.

probe.question: Does a 13-year-old need to worry about eating very salty chips daily?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only old people get problems from salt.

misconceptions.root_belief: Diet-related diseases only concern older people

misconceptions.statement: If I do not add salt at the table, I am not eating much salt.
misconceptions.why: Students think of salt only as what they sprinkle themselves.
misconceptions.fix: Most salt comes from processed and packaged foods like chips, pickles, bread, instant noodles and sauces, not just salt added at the table.

probe.question: A boy never uses the salt shaker but eats instant noodles and chips daily. Is his salt intake low?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because he never adds salt himself.

misconceptions.root_belief: Only visibly added ingredients count toward intake

misconceptions.statement: Sodium and salt are two different things, so low-sodium means a food has no salt at all.
misconceptions.why: Labels list sodium, and students do not know that salt is sodium chloride.
misconceptions.fix: Salt is sodium chloride; sodium is the part in it that affects blood pressure. Salt in grams is about 2.5 times sodium in grams.

probe.question: A packet says 'sodium 400 mg'. Does it contain no salt?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, sodium is different from salt so it has no salt.

misconceptions.source_hint: WHO sodium and salt conversion; food label guides

misconceptions.statement: Fried food made in vegetable oil is healthy because oil comes from plants.
misconceptions.why: Students link 'vegetable' with healthy and ignore calories in oil.
misconceptions.fix: All oils are high in fat and calories, and food absorbs oil during frying. Reused oil can also form harmful trans fats. Fried snacks should be eaten only occasionally.

probe.question: Is a samosa fried in vegetable oil a healthy daily snack?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, vegetable oil is from plants so it is healthy.

misconceptions.source_hint: WHO healthy diet fact sheet; FSSAI Eat Right India

misconceptions.statement: Only fat people need to worry about eating junk food.
misconceptions.why: Students judge health by body size and assume a thin body means a healthy diet.
misconceptions.fix: Thin people can also have high sugar, salt and fat intakes, which can harm the heart and raise diabetes risk. Body size does not show diet quality.

probe.question: A thin boy eats chips and cold drinks daily. Is his diet healthy?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, he is thin so junk food cannot hurt him.

misconceptions.root_belief: Body weight shows how healthy someone is
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO obesity and malnutrition fact sheets

misconceptions.statement: Diabetes spreads from one person to another like a cold.
misconceptions.why: Students treat all illnesses as infections that pass through touch or sharing food.
misconceptions.fix: Diabetes is not infectious. It develops from the body's problem in controlling blood sugar, linked to genes, diet, weight and activity.

probe.question: Can you get diabetes by sitting next to a diabetic classmate?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it can spread through close contact.

misconceptions.root_belief: All diseases are infectious and catching

misconceptions.statement: If the label says 'no added sugar' or lists only 'glucose syrup' or 'jaggery', the food has no sugar worth counting.
misconceptions.why: Students look only for the word 'sugar' and trust natural-sounding names.
misconceptions.fix: Sugar appears as glucose syrup, fructose, dextrose, maltose, honey and jaggery; these all count as free sugars. Check total sugar on the nutrition label.

probe.question: A biscuit lists glucose syrup and honey but not 'sugar'. Is it sugar-free?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the word sugar is not in the ingredients.

misconceptions.root_belief: Only the exact word counts, not other names
misconceptions.source_hint: FSSAI labelling guidance; WHO free sugar definition

misconceptions.statement: Sugar limits mean a person may eat a lot of sugar as long as it is not in tea.
misconceptions.why: Students think the limit only applies to spoon sugar they add.
misconceptions.fix: The limit covers all free sugars in food and drinks, including sweets, biscuits, juices and sauces. WHO advises under 10% of energy, about 6 to 12 teaspoons a day.

probe.question: A girl takes no sugar in tea but eats sweets, biscuits and a cold drink daily. Is she within the limit?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, she does not add sugar to her tea.

misconceptions.root_belief: Only visibly spooned sugar counts toward limits
